passages.t: Moses' seat, and the titles Jesus' followers must not take
passages.happening:
Jesus speaks to the crowds and to his disciples. “The scribes and Pharisees sit in Moses’ seat. So practice and observe everything they tell you. But do not do what they do, for they do not practice what they preach” (verses 2-3).

They tie up heavy loads and put them on other people's shoulders, but will not lift a finger to move them. Everything they do is done to be seen. They make their phylacteries broad and their tassels long. They love the best places at banquets, the chief seats in the synagogues, greetings in the marketplaces, and being called ‘Rabbi’.

Then Jesus turns to his own followers. “But you are not to be called ‘Rabbi,’ for you have one Teacher, and you are all brothers” (verse 8). Call no one on earth your father, for you have one Father in heaven. Do not be called instructors, for you have one Instructor, the Christ. “The greatest among you shall be your servant” (verse 11). Whoever exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted.
passages.hearers:
This is the hardest chapter in Matthew, and it has been badly misused. Read it as what it is. Jesus is a Jew, speaking in the temple courts of Jerusalem, to Jewish crowds and his Jewish disciples, about Jewish teachers of his own day. He speaks the way Israel's own prophets spoke to Israel's leaders.

Notice how he begins. He does not tell the crowds to ignore the Pharisees' teaching. He tells them to keep it. ‘Moses' seat’ was the place from which the law was taught. His charge is that some who teach it do not live it.

The scribes were trained experts in the law of Moses. The Pharisees were a movement, mostly of lay people, who tried to keep God's law in ordinary life. More is said about them in the next passage.

Phylacteries were small leather boxes holding verses of Scripture, which Jewish men tied on the arm and the forehead, taking the command of Deuteronomy 6:8 at its word. Tassels hung from the corners of a garment, as the law commanded. Jesus wore them himself: the woman who was healed touched ‘the fringe of His cloak’ (9:20), and the Greek word there is the one used here for tassels. He is not mocking either custom. He is warning against making them bigger to be seen.

‘Rabbi’ means ‘my great one’ or ‘my teacher’. It was a respectful way to speak to a teacher.

The sharpest part of the passage, verses 8 to 12, is aimed not at the Pharisees but at Jesus' own disciples. They are not to take the titles and the seats of honour he has just described.
passages.ot:
The law commanded both things Jesus mentions. On God's words: “Tie them as reminders on your hands and bind them on your foreheads” (Deuteronomy 6:8). On tassels: they were to be worn “so that you may remember all the commandments of the LORD, that you may obey them” (Numbers 15:39). The tassel was meant to remind the wearer to obey, not to show others how holy he was.

The prophets held teachers to account in the same way. Malachi said, “the lips of a priest should preserve knowledge,” and then charged the priests of his day: “your instruction has caused many to stumble” (Malachi 2:7-8).
passages.hard:
What does ‘practice and observe everything they tell you’ mean, when Jesus has argued with the Pharisees all through the Gospel? Readers have answered in a few ways. Many take it plainly: when the Pharisees teach what Moses taught, keep it, and do not copy their lives. Some think Jesus means the law as read from Moses' seat, not every tradition added to it, since elsewhere he rejects traditions that set aside God's command (15:3-6). Others hear in it a sharp edge, as if to say: even by their own teaching they stand judged. All agree on the point Matthew presses: a teacher's words can be right while the teacher's life is wrong.

Does ‘call no one on earth your father’ forbid calling a priest ‘Father’, or a teacher ‘Doctor’? Christians differ. Catholic and Orthodox Christians call their priests ‘Father’, and point out that Paul calls himself the father of the believers in Corinth: “in Christ Jesus I became your father through the gospel” (1 Corinthians 4:15). Many Protestants avoid such titles in church for this reason. Most readers on every side agree that Jesus is not banning a word. He is forbidding any title that puts a teacher in the place that belongs to God and to Christ, or that lifts one believer above the others. ‘You are all brothers.’

If your own father was absent, or hurt you, this verse is not asking you to pretend otherwise. It tells you that you have a Father in heaven who is not like that.
passages.asks: Jesus' warning lands first on those who teach and lead in his church today, who also have titles, robes and seats of honour. Ask whether you love being seen as godly more than being godly. Ask whose loads you put on others' shoulders without lifting a finger. And ask where you could be a servant this week instead of a great one.

passages.t: Woe to you: the first woes, and who the Pharisees were
passages.happening:
Now Jesus speaks a row of ‘woes’. “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, you hypocrites! You shut the kingdom of heaven in men’s faces. You yourselves do not enter, nor will you let in those who wish to enter” (verse 13).

The next woe: they cross land and sea to win a single convert, and when he becomes one, they make him twice as much a son of hell as they are themselves (verse 15).

You may notice that your Bible skips from verse 13 to verse 15. Verse 14, a woe on those who ‘devour widows' houses’ and make long prayers for show, is missing from the oldest manuscripts. It matches Mark 12:40 and Luke 20:47 and was probably copied in from there. Without it, Matthew has seven woes.
passages.hearers:
A ‘woe’ is a cry of grief and warning, like ‘Alas for you’. It is how Israel's prophets spoke when they saw judgment coming on people they belonged to. It is not a curse, and it is not a shout of triumph.

A ‘hypocrite’ was first a Greek word for an actor on a stage, someone wearing a mask. Jesus uses it for anyone whose religion is a part played for an audience.

Who were the Pharisees? Here it matters to get them right. They were a movement of devout Jews, most of them not priests but lay people, who tried to keep God's law in the whole of ordinary life, at home and at work, not only in the temple. The Jewish historian Josephus says they were the most popular of the Jewish groups and had great influence with ordinary people (Antiquities 18.15). They believed in the resurrection of the dead. Some of them warned Jesus that Herod Antipas wanted to kill him (Luke 13:31). Nicodemus was a Pharisee (John 3:1). So was Gamaliel, “a teacher of the law who was honored by all the people” (Acts 5:34). So was Paul, who said of himself, “as to the law, a Pharisee” (Philippians 3:5).

So ‘Pharisee’ is not a word for a hypocrite. In later Christian speech it came to mean that, but it did not mean that to Jesus' hearers. Jesus argued with the Pharisees because they were close to him. They cared about the same things: the Sabbath, purity, how to keep the law with the whole heart. His woes are aimed at the hypocrisy he saw in some of them, not at a whole movement, still less at a people.

Jewish teachers themselves criticized hypocrisy in their own ranks. Later Jewish teachers spoke in much the same way about teachers who do not practise what they preach. The Babylonian Talmud, put together several centuries after Jesus, lists seven kinds of Pharisee, and treats six of them as false, from the man who makes a show of his good deeds to the man who keeps a tally of them. Only the one who serves God from love is praised. It also tells of a king who warned his wife not to fear the Pharisees, but the hypocrites who imitate them (Sotah 22b).

‘Convert’ here means a non-Jew who became a Jew. Scholars debate how much Jews of Jesus' day sought out converts. Some think the verse means winning a person over to the Pharisees' own way. The point is the same: zeal to win people is worth nothing if they are made worse.
passages.ot:
The woes are an old prophetic form. Isaiah cried six woes over the people of Judah in a single chapter, beginning, “Woe to you who add house to house and join field to field until no place is left and you live alone in the land” (Isaiah 5:8), and, “Woe to those who call evil good and good evil” (Isaiah 5:20). Amos cried, “Woe to those at ease in Zion” (Amos 6:1). Ezekiel spoke against Israel's leaders: “Woe to the shepherds of Israel, who only feed themselves!” (Ezekiel 34:2). And Jeremiah: “Woe to the shepherds who destroy and scatter the sheep of My pasture!” (Jeremiah 23:1).

These prophets were Jews speaking to their own people, often harder than anything in Matthew 23. No one reads Isaiah or Jeremiah as enemies of Israel. Jesus speaks in their line.
passages.hard:
Has this chapter been used against Jewish people? Yes, for centuries. Christians read the woes as a verdict on the whole Jewish people for all time, and used them to teach contempt for Jews and Judaism. That reading is wrong, and this site rejects it plainly.

The woes are a warning to religious leaders, never a verdict on the Jewish people. They are spoken by a Jew to Jewish leaders of one generation, in the voice of Israel's own prophets, and the chapter ends not in triumph but in tears over Jerusalem (verse 37). Some scholars also note that ancient teachers, Jewish and Greek alike, often spoke of rival schools in harsh terms like these, so the words should not be read as a calm description of every Pharisee.

Scholars differ on how much the chapter's sharpness reflects Jesus' own words and how much it reflects the bitter quarrel, after AD 70, between Matthew's community and other Jewish leaders. Christians who hold these are Jesus' words can agree that he spoke them as Jeremiah spoke to Jerusalem: from inside, and with grief.

And the woes fall first on religious leaders of every age, Christian ones included. Every warning here, against loving titles, laying burdens on others, keeping up appearances and shutting people out, has fitted Christian pastors, priests and teachers. The New Testament says that “it is time for judgment to begin with the family of God” (1 Peter 4:17), and that “we who teach will be judged more strictly” (James 3:1). The chapter is rightly read when a Christian reader finds himself in it first.
passages.asks: It is easy to read these woes as being about someone else. Jesus means them for anyone whose faith has become a performance. Ask where you might be shutting the door on someone who wants to come to God: by your judgment, your rules, or your example. And ask what kind of person the people you influence are becoming.

passages.t: Woe to blind guides: oaths that mean nothing
passages.happening:
“Woe to you, blind guides!” Jesus says (verse 16). They teach that if someone swears by the temple, it means nothing, but if he swears by the gold of the temple, he is bound by his oath. “You blind fools!” Which is greater, the gold or the temple that makes it sacred? They say the same about swearing by the altar and swearing by the gift on it. Which is greater, the gift or the altar that makes it sacred?

So, Jesus says, whoever swears by the altar swears by it and by everything on it. Whoever swears by the temple swears by it and by the One who lives in it. And whoever swears by heaven swears by God's throne and by the One who sits on it.
passages.hearers:
An oath was a solemn promise made in God's name, and the law said such a promise must be kept. As this passage shows, people sometimes swore by something close to God instead of by God's name: heaven, the temple, the altar.

The problem Jesus attacks is a set of rules for deciding which oaths ‘count’. Swear by the temple, and you can wriggle out. Swear by the gold of the temple, and you are bound. Rules like that let a person sound solemn while keeping a way out. Jesus says every such oath still reaches God, because the temple, the altar and heaven all belong to him.

He had already gone further in the Sermon on the Mount: “I tell you not to swear at all” (5:34). “Simply let your ‘Yes’ be ‘Yes,’ and your ‘No,’ ‘No’” (5:37). A person whose word can be trusted needs no special oath.

‘Blind guides’ is a bitter picture. A guide's whole job is to see the road for others.
passages.ot: The law took promises to God seriously: “If you make a vow to the LORD your God, do not be slow to keep it, because He will surely require it of you” (Deuteronomy 23:21). The third commandment forbade misusing God's name (Exodus 20:7).
passages.asks: Jesus cares about plain honesty. Ask whether you keep little ways out of your promises: the small print, the words that sound like a yes but are not quite one. Would the people who know you best say your word can be trusted without an oath?

passages.t: Woe: tithes and justice, the cup, and the whitewashed tombs
passages.happening:
“Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, you hypocrites! You pay tithes of mint, dill, and cumin. But you have disregarded the weightier matters of the law: justice, mercy, and faithfulness” (verse 23). They should have done the weightier things without neglecting the others. “You blind guides! You strain out a gnat but swallow a camel” (verse 24).

Woe to them: they clean the outside of the cup and dish, but inside they are full of greed and self-indulgence. “Blind Pharisee! First clean the inside of the cup and dish, so that the outside may become clean as well” (verse 26).

Woe to them: they are like whitewashed tombs, which look beautiful on the outside but inside are full of dead men's bones and every kind of impurity. In the same way, they look righteous on the outside, but inside are full of hypocrisy and wickedness.
passages.hearers:
A tithe was a tenth of a harvest given to God. The law asked for a tenth of grain, wine and oil. Some careful Jews tithed even the herbs from their kitchen gardens, mint, dill and cumin. Notice that Jesus does not mock this. He says they should not neglect it. His charge is that they took care over the herbs and neglected justice and mercy.

The picture is of straining a drink to catch a gnat, a tiny insect, because small creatures were unclean under the law. The camel was the biggest unclean animal anyone in that land knew. The picture is meant to be funny: a man fussing over a gnat in his cup, then swallowing a whole camel, hump and all.

The cup and the dish are a picture of a person. Jesus says the inside that matters is the heart.

Touching a grave made a person unclean for seven days, so graves were marked to warn people away. The Mishnah, written down around AD 200, says that on the fifteenth day of the month Adar, about a month before Passover, the graves were marked (Shekalim 1:1), so that no one would touch one by mistake. Jesus' picture is of a tomb painted white. It looks clean and bright, but the white is there to warn that death is inside.
passages.ot:
Jesus' ‘weightier matters’ echo the prophets. Micah asked, “what does the LORD require of you but to act justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with your God?” (Micah 6:8). Hosea said for God, “For I desire mercy, not sacrifice” (Hosea 6:6), a verse Matthew has quoted twice already (9:13; 12:7).

The law named the camel as unclean (Leviticus 11:4) and every small creature that moves along the ground (Leviticus 11:41). And it said that anyone who touches “a human bone or a grave, will be unclean for seven days” (Numbers 19:16).

Ezekiel used whitewash as a picture of false comfort. He condemned prophets who cried peace when there was no peace, “whitewashing any flimsy wall that is built” (Ezekiel 13:10).
passages.asks: It is possible to be careful about small things and careless about great ones. Ask what your ‘mint and dill’ are: the habits that make you feel faithful. Then ask about justice, mercy and faithfulness. Who in your life needs justice, or mercy, from you? And if your outside looks clean, ask God to deal with the inside first.

passages.t: The tombs of the prophets, and all the righteous blood
passages.happening:
“Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, you hypocrites! You build tombs for the prophets and decorate the monuments of the righteous” (verse 29). They say that if they had lived in their fathers' days, they would not have helped shed the prophets' blood. So, Jesus says, they testify against themselves that they are the sons of those who murdered the prophets. “Fill up, then, the measure of the sin of your fathers” (verse 32). “You snakes! You brood of vipers!”

Jesus says he is sending them prophets and wise men and teachers. Some they will kill and crucify, others they will flog in their synagogues and hound from town to town. “And so upon you will come all the righteous blood shed on earth, from the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of Zechariah son of Berechiah, whom you murdered between the temple and the altar” (verse 35). “Truly I tell you, all these things will come upon this generation” (verse 36).
passages.hearers:
Jesus' words show that tombs of prophets and holy people were being built and decorated in his day, as a way of honouring them. His point is sharp. It is easy to honour dead prophets. It is harder to listen to living ones. The leaders say ‘our fathers’ killed the prophets and claim they would never have done the same. Jesus answers that they are about to do it, to him and to those he sends.

‘Sons’ here means people who follow the same path, as when John the Baptist called the Pharisees and Sadducees a ‘brood of vipers’ (3:7). It is a charge about what they are doing, not a claim that guilt is passed down in the blood.

Abel was the first person murdered in the Bible (Genesis 4). The Zechariah killed ‘between the temple and the altar’ is most likely the priest stoned in the temple court in the days of King Joash (2 Chronicles 24:20-22). In the usual order of the Hebrew Bible, Chronicles comes last, though scholars debate whether that order was already fixed in Jesus' day. So ‘from Abel to Zechariah’ means from the first murder in Scripture to the last, the whole story of righteous people killed. (The order of books in most Christian Bibles is different, so this is easy to miss.)

‘This generation’ means the people alive in Jesus' day. Jesus says the judgment he warns of will fall within their lifetime. Many readers link it to the fall of Jerusalem and the burning of the temple in AD 70, which Jesus foretells in the next verses (24:2).
passages.ot:
When Cain killed Abel, God said, “The voice of your brother’s blood cries out to Me from the ground” (Genesis 4:10). Zechariah son of Jehoiada said as he died, “May the LORD see this and call you to account” (2 Chronicles 24:22). Both deaths cried out for justice.

The law and the prophets were also clear that guilt is not inherited. “Fathers shall not be put to death for their children, nor children for their fathers; each is to die for his own sin” (Deuteronomy 24:16). Ezekiel said, “A son will not bear the iniquity of his father” (Ezekiel 18:20).
passages.hard:
Who was ‘Zechariah son of Berechiah’? The priest killed in the temple court was Zechariah son of Jehoiada (2 Chronicles 24:20). Zechariah son of Berechiah was the prophet whose book stands near the end of the Old Testament (Zechariah 1:1), and the Bible does not tell how he died. Luke's version says only ‘Zechariah’ (Luke 11:51). Skeptics have long called this a plain mistake, and many scholars think Matthew, or the tradition he used, merged the two men. Others offer different explanations. Some think ‘son of Berechiah’ was added by an early copyist: Jerome, writing around 398, reported that the Gospel used by a group of Jewish Christians, the Nazarenes, read ‘son of Jehoiada’ here, and one major old manuscript lacks the words in its first hand. Some suggest Jehoiada had a second name, though there is no evidence of it. A few have pointed to a Zechariah son of Baris whom Josephus says was murdered by Zealots ‘in the middle of the temple’ during the war with Rome (Jewish War 4.343), but most reject this, since Jesus speaks of a murder already done. Christians who hold a high view of Scripture are found on more than one side here, and these notes do not choose. The point is clear on every view: all the righteous blood, from first to last, comes to its reckoning.

Does verse 35 mean that the Jewish people carry the guilt of these murders, then or now? No. Jesus is speaking to leaders of his own day about what they themselves are about to do, and of a judgment that will fall in that generation. Scripture forbids putting the guilt of fathers on children (Deuteronomy 24:16). For centuries many Christians called the Jewish people ‘Christ-killers’ and used scenes like this to justify contempt, expulsions, and violence against Jews. That reading is false, and Christians must reject it plainly. In 1965 the Catholic Church's Second Vatican Council said that what happened in the passion ‘cannot be charged against all the Jews, without distinction, then alive, nor against the Jews of today’. Most churches teach the same. The New Testament places all people inside the guilt: in Acts the first Christians pray that Herod, Pilate, the Gentiles, and the people of Israel all stood together against Jesus (Acts 4:27).
passages.asks: It is easy to honour the prophets of the past and say we would have listened. Ask who is telling you the truth today that you do not want to hear, and how you are treating them. Then ask where you have built a fine monument to someone else's faith while refusing to follow it yourself.

passages.t: O Jerusalem, Jerusalem: the hen and her chicks
passages.happening:
The woes end in a lament. “O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, who kills the prophets and stones those sent to her, how often I have longed to gather your children together, as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, but you were unwilling!” (verse 37).

“Look, your house is left to you desolate” (verse 38). Jesus says they will not see him again until they say, “Blessed is He who comes in the name of the Lord” (verse 39).
passages.hearers:
This is how the chapter of woes ends: not with anger, but with longing. The one who has spoken the woes speaks as someone who loves the city and grieves over it. Luke tells that as Jesus came near Jerusalem, “He wept over it” (Luke 19:41).

A hen gathering her chicks under her wings is one of the tenderest pictures in the Gospels. A hen is not a strong animal. When danger comes, she spreads her wings and puts her own body between her chicks and the threat. Jesus says he has longed to do that for Jerusalem ‘how often’.

‘Your house’ may mean the temple, or the city, or both. In the next verse Jesus leaves the temple for the last time in Matthew, and he tells his disciples that not one stone of it will be left on another (24:1-2).

The last words come from Psalm 118, the psalm the crowds sang as Jesus rode in (21:9).
passages.ot:
The picture of God's wings is old. Boaz blessed Ruth by “the God of Israel, under whose wings you have taken refuge” (Ruth 2:12). A psalm promises, “He will cover you with His feathers; under His wings you will find refuge” (Psalm 91:4).

The warning about the house echoes Jeremiah, who spoke God's words over the king's house: “this house will become a pile of rubble” (Jeremiah 22:5), and, “I have forsaken My house; I have abandoned My inheritance” (Jeremiah 12:7). Jeremiah also wept over his people: “Oh, that my head were a spring of water, and my eyes a fountain of tears!” (Jeremiah 9:1).

The last line is Psalm 118:26: “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the LORD.”
passages.hard:
What does ‘until you say, Blessed is He who comes’ mean? Readers take it in more than one way. Many hear hope in it: a day will come when Jerusalem will welcome Jesus with the words of the psalm. Paul too hoped for a turning of his own people to Christ, and grieved for them: “I have deep sorrow and unceasing anguish in my heart” (Romans 9:2). Others read it as a warning that the city will next see him when he comes as judge, and will have to own him then. Some hold both. These notes do not choose. All agree that the words are spoken with love, not hatred.

This lament also shows how the whole chapter should be read. The woes were not spoken by an enemy standing outside Israel. They were spoken by a Jew who loved Jerusalem and wept over it.
passages.asks: Jesus' last word to the city was not ‘I am done with you’ but ‘How often I have longed to gather you’. If you have been unwilling, hear that he still longs to gather you under his wings. And if you have been hard on people who have hurt you or refused you, ask whether your hardest words come with tears, as his did.
